episode.title_working: The Flood That Wasn't a Flood
episode.place: Buffalo Creek Hollow, Logan County, West Virginia
episode.trigger_event: Failure of Pittston Coal's Dam 3 coal slurry impoundment

foreknowledge.narration: In 1967, the United States Department of the Interior told officials in West Virginia that the impoundments on Buffalo Creek were unstable and dangerous. It was not a lone observation about one bad dam. The same warning covered twenty-nine other structures across the state. The dams were not rebuilt.

foreknowledge.document_name: a partial collapse of one of the Buffalo Creek dams
foreknowledge.prediction: nothing was predicted — the hollow simply flooded, five years early, as a demonstration
foreknowledge.response: State officials asked for a few minor alterations

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

foreknowledge.narration: That same year, one of the Buffalo Creek dams partially gave way. The hollow flooded. Nobody was killed, and afterwards the state asked the company to make a few minor alterations. What had happened, in effect, was a demonstration. Five years early, on a small scale, the valley was shown exactly what these structures did when they failed. The lesson was recorded and filed.

foreknowledge.prediction: that a structure holding back 132 million gallons above seventeen inhabited communities had never actually been designed by anybody
foreknowledge.response: There was no engineering file. All three impoundments were built with almost no engineering involvement, and the only plan for Impoundment 3 was a sketch drawn by the on-site vice president

source.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

foreknowledge.narration: Then there is the question of who designed Impoundment 3, and the answer is that essentially nobody did. All three impoundments were built with almost no engineering involvement at all. There were no load calculations, no material specifications, no analysis of what three days of rain would do. The only plan that existed for Impoundment 3 — a structure holding back a hundred and thirty-two million gallons above seventeen inhabited communities — was a sketch, drawn by the vice president who ran the site.

foreknowledge.prediction: none — the impoundment was declared satisfactory

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

foreknowledge.narration: And four days before it broke, a federal inspector from the Bureau of Mines looked at Dam 3 and wrote down that it was satisfactory.

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: It starts with rain. On the twenty-third of February, rain begins falling across the watershed above Buffalo Creek, and it does not stop. It keeps falling through the twenty-fourth. It is still falling on the twenty-fifth.

timeline.event: the water behind Dam 3 is climbing one to two inches every hour

source.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: By the twenty-fifth, the water behind Dam 3 is no longer just high. It is climbing. One to two inches, every hour. That is a number somebody has to be standing there measuring, which means that by the twenty-fifth somebody is standing there measuring it.

timeline.event: a Buffalo Mining Company vice president is alerted that the impoundment is filling, and so are police in the valley below

source.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: That evening, a vice president of the Buffalo Mining Company is told the impoundment is filling. The police in the valley below are told as well. At this point the disaster is still entirely preventable. There are hours left, a road out, and enough daylight to use it.

timeline.event: word travels down the hollow that the water has almost reached the top of the dam, and families sit up in their houses, awake, waiting

source.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: Word travels down the hollow anyway, the way it does in a place where everyone works for the same company. The water is nearly at the top of the dam. Families sit up through the night in their houses, dressed, listening to rain on the roof, waiting to be told something.

timeline.display_time: half past one in the morning
timeline.event: the water behind Dam 3 stands exactly one foot below the crest

source.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: At half past one in the morning, the water behind Dam 3 stands exactly one foot below the crest.

timeline.event: the vice president orders every effort to warn residents stopped, and tells the police that the dam will hold

source.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: And in the hours that follow, the vice president orders every effort to warn residents stopped. He tells the police the dam will hold. The people sitting up in their houses are not told to leave. The last piece of useful information anyone had was withdrawn while they waited for it.

measurement.unit: gallons of water, coal refuse and silt

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: At approximately eight in the morning, Dam 3 gives way. A hundred and thirty-two million gallons of water, coal refuse and silt come out of the head of the hollow at once.

timeline.event: the black wave reaches the two impoundments below it and plows straight through both

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: Two minutes later it reaches the two impoundments below. Neither slows it. It plows straight through both of them and takes their contents with it, so the wave that continues down the valley is larger than the one that started.

timeline.event: Saunders, the community nearest the dams, is struck first, and ceases to exist

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: Saunders is nearest, and Saunders goes first. Not damaged. Not flooded. The community is removed from the ground it stood on.

timeline.event: Pardee, Lorado, Craneco and Lundale are hit in sequence as the water runs the length of the hollow

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: Then it runs. Pardee. Lorado. Craneco. Lundale. The wave moves down the single road that every one of these places was built along, and there is no sideways to go, because a hollow has walls.

timeline.event: Stowe, Crites, Latrobe, Robinette and Amherstdale follow

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: Stowe. Crites. Latrobe. Robinette. Amherstdale. By now people downstream can hear it before they can see it — a sound that survivors describe as unlike anything else, arriving several seconds ahead of the water.

timeline.display_time: three hours from the first breach
timeline.event: seventeen communities have been demolished or partly destroyed, ending at Kistler where the hollow opens out

corroborated_by.title: Buffalo Creek Dam (West Virginia, 1972) — Dam Failures and Lessons Learned

timeline.narration: Three hours from the first breach, it is over. Seventeen communities have been demolished or partly destroyed along sixteen miles of valley, ending at Kistler where the hollow finally opens out and the water spreads and loses its strength.

people.narration: Shirley Marcum lived in the hollow, and she survived. What she remembers afterwards is not the water. It is the warning system that Buffalo Creek actually had that morning — which was not a siren, not a telephone tree, not the company, and not the police. In her account, a neighbour spotted it, pulled her car up in front of the house, and shouted. Her words: "The only warning we had was just a neighbor woman had spotted it and just pulled in front of our house and hollered, 'Run, the dam has broke!'" That was the alarm. A woman in a car, shouting. Everything upstream — the measurements, the vice president, the police who had been told the night before — produced nothing that reached these houses. The warning that saved lives in the hollow was one neighbour deciding, on her own, to stop and shout.

people.narration: The engineering record for Impoundment 3 names one man: Steve Dasovich, the vice president on site. He is named because of a document he produced. Not a design review, not a stability analysis, not a specification for the material the structure was made of. A sketch. That was the plan for a wall of coal waste holding back a hundred and thirty-two million gallons of water above seventeen towns full of sleeping people. It is worth sitting with how ordinary that was. Nobody hid it. There was no cover-up at the design stage, because there was no design stage. The company built the thing the way you build a rubbish heap, and the state of West Virginia looked at it and let it stand.

aftermath.narration: A hundred and twenty-five people were killed. One thousand one hundred and twenty-one were injured. Over four thousand were left homeless — in a valley whose entire population was around five thousand. More than five hundred homes were destroyed. Seventeen communities were demolished or partly destroyed along sixteen miles of hollow. Those numbers describe a place that did not simply lose buildings. Buffalo Creek lost the thing that made it a set of communities rather than a set of addresses, and the sociologist who studied it afterwards found survivors describing their own valley as dead — not because the ground was gone, but because everyone who had made it a place was scattered across temporary housing and never came back together.

Its conclusion was that Pittston had shown flagrant disregard for the safety of the people living below its impoundments.

reckoning.narration: Six months after the failure, Congress passed the National Dam Inspection Act, requiring an inventory and inspection of dams across the United States. It took a hundred and twenty-five deaths in one West Virginia valley to produce a law that counted how many other structures like it existed. The answer, once anyone finally counted, was thousands.

voice.1: February 26th, 1972. Just before eight in the morning in Logan County, West Virginia. It has been raining on the mountains above Buffalo Creek for three days, and at the head of the hollow, behind a pile of coal waste, 132 million gallons of black water are sitting one foot below the top of something nobody ever engineered. Below it, along sixteen miles of single road, five thousand people are asleep. Some of them are not. Some of them have been awake all night.
voice.3: One hundred and thirty-two million gallons. Seventeen communities. Three hours from the first breach to the last.
voice.4: But the rain was not the threat. What came down that hollow was not a flood, and calling it one has always been the most useful lie in this story. It was a refuse pile. Built without a plan, held up by nothing anyone had calculated, and inspected four days earlier by a man who wrote down that it was satisfactory. The water had been rising for two days and the company knew. The police knew. And in the last hours before it broke, a company vice president told them to stop warning people, because the dam would hold.
voice.6: To understand what happens at Buffalo Creek, you first have to understand what was actually sitting above those houses, because it was not a reservoir and it was not a dam. Coal does not come out of a mountain clean. It comes out mixed with rock and clay and dirt, and before anyone will buy it, it has to be washed. Washing it produces two things. It produces coal, and it produces an enormous volume of black slurry — water, silt, and crushed rock with no value to anybody. That waste has to be put somewhere, and in the West Virginia coalfields the somewhere was almost always the nearest hollow. A company would tip its refuse across a stream, day after day, year after year, until the pile itself was tall enough to hold water back. And then the water would collect behind it. That is the entire design. Nobody calculated the load. Nobody specified the material. Nobody asked what would happen when three days of rain arrived at once. The structure was a byproduct of throwing rubbish away, which happened to be holding back a lake, above people's houses. Now understand the shape of the ground. Buffalo Creek is a hollow — a narrow valley with steep sides, one road running its length, and a string of coal towns strung along that road wherever the ground was flat enough to build. Saunders sat nearest the top. Then Pardee, Lorado, Craneco, Lundale, Stowe, Crites, Latrobe, Robinette, Amherstdale, Becco, Fanco, Riley, Braeholm, Accoville, Crown, and at the bottom, Kistler. Sixteen miles of them. There is no high ground in a hollow. There is nowhere to go sideways. And water released at the top does not spread out and lose its strength the way it would across open country. It is funnelled. It arrives at the bottom concentrated instead of dispersed, and it arrives fast. Pittston had three refuse dams stacked in the Middle Fork above all of it. Dam 3 was the newest, the highest, and the one holding the water.
voice.9:
And the rain kept coming.
By then the decision had already been made — by nobody making one.
Upstream, a man was watching the water climb and doing the arithmetic in his head.
The people in the houses below had been given the only piece of information that mattered, and then it had been taken back.
It held until it didn't.
voice.12: The rain didn't destroy Buffalo Creek. It only found out what Pittston had built above it, and what the state had agreed not to look at.
